title: Super growth outpaces property
full_text:
Superannuation has started to separate from the property market as a generator of household wealth with its growth outpacing the latter by the widest margin in six years, according to analysis carried out by SuperConcepts.
The administration provider noted superannuation grew by 5.2 per cent in the June quarter 2026, while residential land and dwellings fell 0.3 per cent, which represented the largest outperformance since June 2020. In dollar terms, super added $231 billion to household wealth, while residential property fell by $34 billion.
While housing is still the larger asset pool at $12.2 trillion, around 2.6 times the size of superannuation at $4.7 trillion, the research noted over the past 20 years household wealth in the latter has grown at a faster rate, at 4.37 times compared to 3.85 times for residential property, and has doubled since 1989, growing from 12.5 per cent to 24.3 per cent over 37 years.
“Given the recent correction in Australian house prices and the legislative changes to property investment through SMSFs, we wanted to understand how the relationship between property and superannuation is changing. Our research shows that super is now moving household wealth independently of the housing market,” SuperConcepts stated.
“Superannuation has crossed a critical threshold as a wealth-holding mechanism independent of property markets. The sector now moves household net worth materially on its own, with limited direct exposure to residential property downside.
“Housing weakness and super strength operating simultaneously indicates the two asset classes are decoupling as wealth drivers, reshaping how Australian households build and retain assets.”
Despite this growth, the firm noted the impact on SMSFs of property price downturns and the prohibition on borrowing to purchase residential property.
“ANZ forecasts a peak-to-trough fall of 10.6 per cent in capital city property prices across 2026 and 2027, equivalent to roughly $1.2 trillion in lost wealth,” it said.
“Super would need to grow approximately 26 per cent to offset a 10 per cent fall in housing wealth, compared to this quarter’s 5.2 per cent growth rate,” it added, noting property assets in Australian Prudential Regulation Authority-regulated funds made up 6.4 per cent of assets compared to 15.9 per cent in SMSFs.
“From 10 August 2026, SMSFs can no longer take on new borrowing to purchase residential property, meaning residential exposure can only decline over time.
“The regulatory shift prohibiting new geared residential property in SMSFs signals a structural shrinking of super’s property holdings over time.”
author: Jason Spits
heading: Superannuation and Investments
